title: The Best GPS Sport Watches (2026 Recommendations Guide)
content:
Here’s my full GPS watch recommendation guide for winter 2026-2027. This accounts for every model released to date, including ones that just came out two days ago. But more critically, it takes into account hundreds of comparison tests/workouts I’ve done this year alone with all these watches, as well as more than 17 years of experience testing GPS sports watches. Every single day I’m testing and comparing GPS watches, even when not working on a specific review. No run or ride goes without at least 3-4 GPS units, sometimes more.

The good news here is that there’s arguably never been a better time to be a consumer of a GPS sports watch. While the bigger brands (e.g., Apple & Garmin) have gotten bigger in recent years, the smaller brands (e.g., COROS & Amazfit) have found ways to offer incredible value in between the product roadmap cracks of the big companies. And all of these companies are effectively pushing each other to compete for your money, by delivering frequent and deep firmware updates – even for older watches.

While I know many of you will skip right to the recommendations, I’d really encourage you to read the next two sections, especially my ‘Rules of Thumb’ one, as there are lots of products to consider, but this might help quickly narrow it down a bit.

The Problem with Most Recommendation Guides:

Most sports watch recommendation guides suck, because they have two core problems:

1) They never used the watches: They’re either written by AI, or written by people who have never touched the watches. They simply read specs, combined with picking the most popular watches, to drive clicks. If you don’t see any real-world non-marketing photos in a recommendation guide, that’s a near-guarantee it’s slop (AI or human). That’s not me. Every device here I’ve tested, written reviews/posts on, and know what’s good and bad about it.

2) They try to appease manufacturers: I’m not here to try and make every manufacturer happy, or every single person happy by ensuring I recommend their watch. You can come here to see my recommendations from someone who has actually used all these things, and likewise, I don’t care if I upset a company because their watch didn’t get included. I’m going to give you recommendations the same as I would for all my friends and family who’ve been texting me over the last few weeks trying to decide on holiday gifts. That won’t include a lot of watches, or a lot of companies. Not everyone is a winner. I will, however, include some honorable mentions in each category.

There’s also one more factor that isn’t so much a problem with all guides, but just a fact of life that I feel like is worth mentioning to address the elephant in the room:

3) Yes, Garmin & Apple are in every category: Look, when you manufacture the most smartwatches in the world (Apple), or you make the most models (Garmin) and are basically the 2nd most popular smartwatch brand out there, you’re going to be in more categories. Especially because these companies make models targeted at the three basic price tiers. In Apple’s case, they have three models. In Garmin’s case, they have 2,328 models. Other companies also have models for each price tier, but tend to do best in one or two price buckets. Nobody beats Garmin’s feature depth at the top end. But equally, Garmin struggles to compete on ‘value’ in the ultra-budget range. Just like Apple struggles to compete on pure sports features across all price buckets, but dominates on integration with the iPhone. Nonetheless, there’s a reason these two companies sell tens of millions of units each year: People genuinely find their products the best/most dependable/compelling. If they sucked, people wouldn’t buy them for long.

If you find these recommendations useful from a real human, and all the time I put into testing things, then please share out this post to your friends and family. It’s as simple as that.

My Rules of Thumb:

When it comes to how I recommend watches to friends and family, there are kinda a few overarching questions to ask yourself first. It’s not a perfect flow chart per se, nor does it cover every edge case, but it gets you to the right overall group of watches to look at. This somewhat sets aside the budget question, and instead focuses on what you want out of a watch.

1) How much battery do you want? Are you looking for a watch that lasts 4+ days on your wrist (in smartwatch mode), or 20+ hours in GPS mode? If so, you’ll basically be skipping Apple/Google/Samsung watches, and focusing more on the Garmin/Suunto/Amazfit/COROS/etc. watches.

2) Do you want a smart watch, or a smarter watch? The definition of a ‘smart watch’ is imperfect and constantly evolving. Both Garmin & Apple make ‘smartwatches’, but I think we’d agree that for daily ‘smarts’ the Apple Watch can do more (whereas inversely, Garmin does more for sports areas). For most people, the biggest definition of a smartwatch is whether you can take phone calls on it. In the case of Apple/Google/Samsung, you can easily make and take phone calls from anyone. Whereas with Garmin’s LTE-based units, you can make phone calls to friends/family, but if your dentist randomly calls, it won’t route to your watch. And then for the rest of Garmin’s watches and Suunto/COROS/Amazfit/etc., you’ll need your phone with you to take that call. There are lots of other smart features beyond that, but that tends to be the biggest one.

3) Keep in the Ecosystem: Next, if you already have one or more devices in the ecosystem of a given company, then generally it works best to keep them in that ecosystem. For example, if you already have a Garmin Edge bike computer, then unless you want a smarter smartwatch, get a Garmin watch. Likewise, if you’re on Android and want the smartest smartwatch available with the best Android integration, then your choices are basically Google & Samsung. For Apple Watches, you need an iPhone, and for Samsung/Google watches, you need an Android phone. For all the other companies, it doesn’t matter, and they support both ecosystems.

4) All these watches do virtually all sport modes: Years ago, I had to write a separate guide for triathletes, a separate one for cyclists, hikers, and so on. But these days, all of these watches have virtually all sport modes. Most companies keep that list nearly identical across all watches. The edge case exceptions tend to be that high-impact watersports (e.g., waterskiing and surfing) tend to be reserved for watches with higher waterproof ratings (due to impact pressures). And likewise, Garmin gatekeeps their triathlon/multisport modes to mid-tier and above watches.

5) If Maps Matter: Specifically, offline maps while doing a sport mode. There’s a bit of a divide here. The default offline maps/navigation on Apple/Google watches aren’t really great for navigation in many cases, as they have limited/no ability to import hiking/etc. routes easily. There are 3rd-party apps that make this much better, though. Meanwhile, Garmin/Suunto/Amazfit/COROS have great offline map options that can easily import in routes from Strava/Komoot/etc. That said, Garmin gatekeeps these to devices that cost $500-$600+ usually (the exception being any Fenix unit on sale has full maps, as does any Forerunner 965/970 unit). Garmin units below that price have no offline maps, but can still do breadcrumb-style routing.

Ok, hopefully that helps a bit, and cleans up the recommendations down below trying to explain all that stuff for each model. So, let’s get into it!

I’ve divided things up into three basic price groupings:

Budget Category: These are watches under $250

Mid-Range Category: These are watches from $250 to $750

Top-End Models: These are watches from $750+

I know, you can probably subdivide that mid-tier more, or you can pretend the budget goes to $300 (it won’t change anything here), but as you’ll see, things all kinda work out. Ultimately, price brackets are simply a way for any recommendation guide to put things in certain buckets. You know your own budget best, and might have a different price ceiling/bracket.

Budget Category (under $250):

It’s amazing to see how freaking good the watches in this category have become. And it’s funny, these four watches all do the basics really well, but each has their own ‘strengths’ in surprisingly different ways. To decide which one is right, I’d defer again to the ‘Rules of Thumb’ section to help narrow it down.

Garmin Forerunner 70:

When Garmin launched the Forerunner 70 this spring, I argued it was one of the best watches they’ve released in many years. Not because it has the most features (it doesn’t), nor because it has the fanciest materials (it doesn’t), but because it was the rare Garmin model where Garmin was clearly going for blood on packing as much as they could into a sub-$250 watch (now $199 on sale). They took almost all their top-end training metrics from their $1,000 watches, and stuffed them in here, price be damned. If you don’t care about offline maps, but want the polish and connectivity of the Garmin ecosystem (including apps), this is probably the best watch for sports folks in this category. The downside is simply that it doesn’t have the offline maps of the COROS Pace 4 or Amazfit (it still has routing/navigation, though), nor does it have the triathlon mode of the COROS Pace 4. And then when it comes to fancier smart features, it doesn’t have those like the Apple Watch.

COROS Pace 4:

COROS made the Pace 4 even better just a few months ago when they surprise-announced they were adding free offline mapping (a year after release!), which is a crazy move for a company to make. This watch does everything you want a GPS running watch to do – from accurate tracking to navigation to daily activity/health tracking, and of course good battery life. But of course, it’s more than just a running watch, as it has modes for hiking, triathlon, cycling, and plenty more sports modes. You won’t ever find sales on COROS products, so the prices are what they are. The main ‘downside’ is that you don’t have apps on the watch like you do on the Garmin/Apple Watch, nor as many integration partners as Garmin/Apple do. Also, the running training metrics here seem to lack any scientific basis, though total training load is fine. Still, if you’re following some other plan and ignore what the watch is telling you to do, this is a great option.

Apple Watch SE 3:

The Apple Watch SE 3 is a great option if you want more of a ‘smarter’ watch than the others, especially if you want to get cellular on it to ditch your phone. Though, if you don’t care about taking calls/texts away from your phone, then the price plummets down to well under sub-$200 on sale. The main benefit of an Apple Watch (for iPhone users) is really the integration with your phone for calls and text messages, especially the ability to answer anyone anywhere. You also get a lot of the wider health tracking features found within the Apple Ecosystem. That said, the downside is you don’t get any of the new ‘Readiness’ features found on the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, because this unit lacks the newer optical HR sensor found on those units. Further, if you’re looking to do navigation/routing, you’ll want to get some 3rd-party app, because the stock one is mostly hot mess territory.

Amazfit Active Max:

If there’s one area that Amazfit dominates in options, it’s the sub-$300 category, but even more so, the sub-$200 category where this and the Active 2/Active 3 live. Those watches are all very similar, and mostly just have slight hardware differences around buttons and screens. But at $120 on sale, the Amazfit Active Max is just insane value. It’s even got full offline mapping (navigation), plus things like structured workout support, as well as a gazillion sport modes (the list is both hilarious and hilariously long, over 170 sports). And of course it does health tracking like everyone else. The main downside to Amazfit isn’t hardware build quality, but software build quality. The company tends to just release model after model, and many of the software features feel a bit unpolished/half-baked. Not usually bad or anything, but clearly rushed. Still, if you can deal with an occasional quirk, the value here is insane.

There are also some honorable mentions here:

Garmin Vivoactive 6: This is a great all-arounder watch, which simply lacks the buttons of the Forerunner 70. But also lacks some of the new training features the Forerunner 70 got, hence why I prefer the Forerunner 70.

 

Garmin Forerunner 170 on sale: The watch is priced just a touch bit higher than the Forerunner 70, but essentially adds some extra hardware bits including offline payments (NFC), as well as offline music (Spotify/etc) in the Music models. I have an entire comparison post here going through all the differences.

 

Amazfit T-Rex 3: This is an awesome watch, which is much more rugged than the Amazfit Active Max. Likewise, the Active 2 and Active 3 are also great options. Seriously, this is a price bucket that Amazfit really delivers on.

 

Suunto Run 1: This unit did really well in my review when it launched, and I think if you view it through the lens of ‘buy it for what it has’ rather than any promise of new features that it won’t get, it can be a really good deal. Suunto just launched their Run 2 watch, but spiked the price well above the COROS Pace 4, making it kinda silly.

Again, there are a lot of good options that can also sneak into this category on sale, but that quickly makes it hard to keep up with.

Mid-Range Watches:

Look, this is a vast price range of $350 to $750. Sure, I could subdivide it up again, or I could shift it from say $400 to $750, but realistically that won’t change anything in the lower tier bucket. Or I could cut the ceiling off at $600, forcing the FR970 into the upper-tier bucket just for the heck of it. There’s no perfect option here. The problem is, in many ways these watches are actually really darn similar in terms of core capabilities; instead, you’re basically paying differences for what you value most. If you value Apple integration, you pay Apple for that. If you value deep sports features, you pay Garmin for that. If you value a little bit of everything while still having money in your wallet, you pay COROS for that.

Apple Watch Series 12:

There’s a reason the Apple Watch is basically the most popular watch in the world – the just-works factor is super high. And the Apple Watch Series 12 continues that tradition, but adds in a bunch of new software features this year focused on trending your daily metrics. That includes heart rate variability tracking, which rolls into a new ‘Readiness’ score (similar to what others already have). But beyond that, it’s the overall smartwatch integration into the Apple ecosystem and health/medical tracking that drives most adoption here. The main downside to the Apple Watch Series 12 continues to be it’s basically 1-1.5 day battery life of course, and then it’s sport profiles are rather simplistic compared to most other companies. It’s great for tracking a run (or doing a structured workout), but if you want to navigate a trail route, it’s a bit messy and will ultimately require a 3rd party app to do well.

Garmin Forerunner 970

The Garmin Forerunner series is legendary among runners, but the thing is, this watch is just as capable a triathlon watch as anything else. In fact, it has virtually all the sport modes of a high-end Fenix 9 series device (save things like diving), and most of the hardware internals – such as the LED flashlight. In many ways, the Garmin Forerunner 970 is referred to as the ‘plastic Fenix’ (much to the chagrin of the Forerunner team…but hey, sometimes the truth hurts). You’re basically trading the fancier materials/case design of the Fenix for nearly identical software on a Forerunner-branded model. But that’s ideal if you want a thinner and lighter model than the Fenix series; plus, it’s less expensive. So why buy this over the COROS Pace 4, which is $300 cheaper? In short, you’re buying a far more polished device/platform with wider integration, better maps, a flashlight, medically certified ECG, and a bunch of other things that don’t fit into a single paragraph. The downside? Really just one thing: The price.

COROS Pace 4 Pro

This is probably one of the best all-arounders in this vast price bucket. The COROS Pace 4 Pro has full offline mapping/navigation, has all the sport modes you might need, it has a big beautiful and brilliant 1.5” AMOLED screen at 3,500 nits, it’s thin and lightweight, and you can even pretend you want to talk to your wrist with its microphone and speaker. This model just came out last month, so it’s going to get updates for quite some time. Not just because it’s new, but because COROS is really good about providing new software feature updates for a really really really long time. More so than anyone else out there, albeit some of those updates are just catching up with what Garmin offers. But hey, it’s updates nonetheless! The main ‘downside’ to the COROS Pace 4 Pro would simply be that the mapping isn’t as deep as Garmin here, and there are no on-device apps like Garmin/Apple.

There are so many honorable mentions here in this category that it could probably deserve its own post:

Google Pixel Watch 5: This one is tricky. If you don’t have an iPhone, but still want smarts, the Pixel Watch 5 is a great option. Seriously, it’s your next best option that’s not Garmin/COROS. And Google did some amazing stuff with software here for GPS accuracy that’s astonishing. And likewise, their Google Health app is doing incredible stuff around AI training recommendations that doesn’t suck (when every other sports AI thing I’ve tried sucks). But when it comes to actually using it for sports, there are still some weird gaps, like the lack of a lap button or the ability to pair a heart rate or other sensors. Further, it lacks sports route/navigation at all.

 

Suunto Race 2: This one is also tricky, as it probably would have made this list a month ago. With the COROS Pace 4 Pro coming along, it sorta sideswipes Suunto out of a win in this category, despite being very similar and priced the same. But this is mainly because the Suunto Race 2 is now a year older, and with Suunto’s new Race 3S being announced, I worry what will happen next year with software updates for the older Race 2 series. Whereas with COROS, they have a very dependable record of software updates for older units. Plus, the display and such is better on the COROS Pace 4 Pro anyway.

 

Garmin Forerunner 570: If you don’t care about mapping, but want Garmin’s other premium running/sports features and a larger display than the Forerunner 70/170, you can grab the Forerunner 570 instead. Or, if you do care about mapping, just get the older Forerunner 965, which people are pretty darn happy with. You just won’t get meaningful new software features on the FR965 like you would with the Forerunner x70 series (e.g., 70/170/570/970) because it’s considered a previous software platform.

 

Garmin Fenix 8 on sale: Right now the Garmin Fenix 8 is at $749 (and occasionally dipping lower). The Fenix 8 series gets virtually all the new Fenix 9 software features, and basically wipes away everyone else in this category from a features standpoint. It’s got certified dive support, the most feature-rich maps of anything here, medically certified ECG, an LED flashlight, and tons more. It’s hard to beat at prices this low.

Top-End Models:

At over $750, there are really only a few options in this realm. You’ve got the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and then you have 28 different Fenix models and variants. There are no other models in this pricing realm that are worth buying.

Garmin Fenix 9 Series:

The Garmin Fenix 9 series is the watch you buy when you want the absolute best option in the market for sports. There’s simply no competition anywhere remotely close to this. Of course, the Fenix 9 has many tiers/pricing available. Right now they start at $899 on sale, but normally $999, and then go up a few hundred dollars more into the $1,100+ range. The three tiers are Base/Pro/Pro inReach. Essentially, Pro adds a brighter display and some other hardware tweaks, whereas Pro inReach adds LTE capability and satellite messaging. Personally, I love the Pro inReach because I know I’ve got a way to get messages to someone outside of cellular range (either for general updates or emergencies). My wife runs all the time for hours by herself at night, and hates carrying a phone, so this works perfectly because I get an LTE LiveTrack link to follow along. Like with the Forerunner 970, the main downside here is price. It’s expensive; there’s no getting around that. The secondary downside of the Pro inReach models is that while they have LTE calling/texts, it’s really focused on keeping your immediate friends/family updated. It doesn’t share a phone number/line with your existing device. So it works well within the limited focus area, but is really about being a super-deep sports watch.

Apple Watch Ultra 4: 

As I noted earlier, Apple makes products in all these categories that are incredibly popular. The reality though, is that you’re purchasing the Apple Watch Ultra 4 not for deep sports features, but for the Apple ecosystem and the longer battery life. I wear the Apple Watch Ultra 4 daily on my wrist (the other wrist has a Garmin Fenix 9 Pro inReach 47mm). What I appreciate about the Apple Watch Ultra 4 isn’t so much the core sports features that it has, nor the diving support it has, nor even the emergency siren I’ll hopefully never use. Instead, I appreciate the iMessage integration and how good it is, as well as other smartphone notification-type features getting full photos and such on my wrist. Certainly, that’s also a function of Apple gatekeeping those features that way within iOS, but until that changes, that’s what I value most from the Apple Watch Ultra 4. The downsides to the Ultra 4 honestly depend a bit on why you’re buying it. If you’re buying it for deep athletic adventures, you might be a bit disappointed with the sports features and mapping/etc. But if you’re buying it to track/run a marathon, it’s awesome.

A few honorable mentions here:

Garmin Enduro 3 or Enduro 4: I just want to briefly mention that if you don’t want to spend the money for a Fenix 9, but want ultra-long battery life, the Enduro 3/Enduro 4 are basically Fenix 8/Fenix 9 models, except without the AMOLED screen and without the diving/speaker/mic features. And in doing so, the price ends up being a heck of a lot cheaper. Likewise, if you don’t want/need the Fenix 9, then check out both the Fenix 8 and Fenix 8 Pro, which share the same software, but just cost less and have slightly less bright displays.

Wrap-Up

Ok, I know there’s a lot to take in above, and frankly, you could sit here and subdivide categories all day long, or tweak recommendations to an individual’s priorities as well. One person might prefer mapping; the other doesn’t care one bit. One person wants a week of battery, the other is fine with one day. One person wants dive support, while another wants climbing support, and so on.

Thus, if you’ve got questions, I’ll try my best in the comments section. Again, my goal above is to provide recommendations as I would to my friends/family, not to try and cover every watch in the market for every possible scenario. But equally, I’m happy to try and answer questions down below to thread the needle in between all the gaps out there!

With that – thanks for reading!
